definition: A false statement made on purpose to damage someone's good name.
example: The novelist spent years trying to clear her grandfather's name of an old calumny.
nuance: Criticism can be true and fair, but calumny is always false and spiteful; don't confuse it with calamity, which means a disaster.
prompt: A baker learns that a rival has been spreading untrue stories about her shop.
options: The rival's calumny, an invented tale about sawdust in her bread, drove customers away.
The calumny of the flood left the bakery's ovens rusted and useless by morning.
Loyal customers heaped calumny on her, calling her pastries the finest in town.
The inspector's calumny correctly noted that her walk-in refrigerator was running two degrees too warm.
reasons: A deliberately false story meant to hurt her business is exactly this kind of attack.
A flood is a disaster, which is calamity; this sentence mixes up the two look-alike words.
Warm praise is the reverse of a lie told to damage someone.
An accurate official finding is not false or malicious, so it cannot be this.

practice.prompt: A retired teacher receives an anonymous letter claiming he once cheated at a chess tournament.
options: He dismissed the letter as calumny, since the tournament records proved he had played fairly.
The town honored his long career by presenting him with a calumny at his retirement dinner.
A calumny struck the school last spring when a burst pipe flooded the gymnasium floor.
His friend offered calumny by gently and truthfully pointing out a weak move in his favorite opening.
reasons: The accusation is untrue and meant to tarnish him, so the label fits.
An honor given at a celebration is a tribute, not a damaging lie.
A burst pipe is a misfortune, which is calamity, not a false accusation.
Kind, honest feedback has none of the falsehood or ill will the word requires.
